pronunciation.approximation: 'AH-nih-moos' — stress the first syllable; the final vowel is short and rounded.
pronunciation.note: Animus is a Latin word, not a Greek proper name. It has no indigenous alphabetic 'original script' other than the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form animus is already the Latin spelling; the restoration capitalises the proper-noun form as a scholarly citation. Because no distinctive diacritic or special letter is added, the entry is Tier 2.

domains.title: Mind, Spirit, and Courage
domains.subtitle: The Active Power of the Soul
domains.lead: Animus is the Latin word for mind, spirit, courage, and sometimes fierce anger. It names the active, directing part of the person: the faculty that thinks, decides, resists, and fights. Where anima is breath and life, animus is will and consciousness. Roman ethics placed great weight on the animus as the seat of virtue, and the word survives in English as a sign of both spiritedness and settled hostility.

mythology.lead: Animus is not a mythological character but a concept that runs through Roman literature, rhetoric, and ethics. Its 'mythology' is the story of how Latin speakers imagined the active self: the mind that commands, the spirit that endures, and the anger that destroys.

myths.title: The Seat of Courage
myths.text:
For Roman writers the animus is the source of virtus, the courage that makes a citizen worth the state. Cicero calls the animus divine — a fragment of the gods' own fire dwelling in the human breast, to be cultivated as our best part (Tusculan Disputations 1.64–66) — and Livy makes the point with a story: Horatius Cocles, holding the bridge alone against Etruria, cries that every man must sooner or later die, and those who die for their country are blessed (Ab Urbe Condita 2.10). The word runs through the whole ethic: magnanimus, great-souled; fortis animo, brave in mind; abicere animum, to throw away one's spirit — the one unforgivable loss.

Roman heroism is interior before it is physical: the legion's discipline was an animus trained in common.

myths.title: The Ruling Faculty
myths.text:
Roman Stoics identified the animus with the hēgemonikon, the ruling part of the soul, and made its governance the whole of philosophy. Seneca's treatise On Anger anatomizes the animus inflamed: wrath, he says, is a brief madness, and the wise man cures it as a doctor cures fever, before it becomes habit (De Ira 1.1–4). Marcus Aurelius, emperor and diarist, began his mornings reminding his ruling faculty what it was and what work lay before it (Meditations 2.1–2). The passions were diseases of the animus; reason its hygiene; tranquility its health. The prize of this medicine was freedom — the only kind Rome could not grant by law: an animus dependent on nothing external, therefore afraid of nothing external.

The Stoic wager is that the will, properly governed, is the one province fortune can never invade.

myths.title: The Wrath of the Mind
myths.text:
Virgil runs the whole moral range of the word through his two heroes. Aeneas is praised for the mind that does not break — 'his mind remains unmoved, his tears fall in vain' as Dido burns, the discipline of grief bent back into duty (Aeneid 4.449). Turnus ends the poem driven by the same word at its worst: resolution curdled into fury, pressing the fight on when the gods have already decided, until the poem's last line closes on a life 'fleeing, indignant, down to the shades' (Aeneid 12). Latin itself declines to choose: animus means both noble resolve and violent temper, and the Aeneid holds both senses up to the light until the reader sees they share one root.

The same inner fire, Virgil says, forges the founder and destroys his last enemy; virtue is animus with a bridle.

myths.title: Jung's Animus
myths.text:
In Jungian psychology the animus is the unconscious masculine image within the female psyche — the inner figure of spirit, word, and argument, just as the anima is the soul-image in the male (Jung, 'The Relations between the Ego and the Unconscious,' Collected Works 7; developed in Aion, CW 9ii). Integrated, he is the woman's bridge to inner discrimination; unintegrated, he possesses her opinions as her own — she is 'animus-ridden,' lectured by a voice she mistakes for herself. Later analysts, notably Marie-Louise von Franz, refined the schema, and feminist critics have reworked or rejected it; but the borrowed Latin word kept its antique aura: the animus is the mind that speaks from within, whether one calls it archetype, inner voice, or conscience.

Twenty centuries after Seneca, the word still names an inner power that must be befriended rather than obeyed.

lore.syncretism: The Latin animus maps onto Greek thymos (spiritedness), nous (mind), and psychē (soul). Roman Stoicism absorbed Greek psychology and gave it a distinctly Roman emphasis on duty, endurance, and public virtue. In modern English 'animus' has narrowed to mean hostility or ill will, but the broader Latin sense survives in words such as animate, magnanimous, and animosity. The word is a bridge between ancient ethics and modern psychology.
lore.culturalLegacy: Animus survives in English as both a technical term and an everyday word. 'Animate,' 'animation,' and 'animal' derive from anima, but 'animus,' 'magnanimous,' 'pusillanimous,' and 'animosity' preserve the masculine, spirited sense. In Jungian psychology the animus is a major archetype, and in law and rhetoric 'animus' still names intention or state of mind. The word's career shows how Roman concepts of mind and courage continue to shape Western languages and thought.
lore.extendedMeditation:
To meditate on Animus is to meditate on the will. The Latin word contains both the noblest and the most dangerous forms of spiritedness: courage and wrath, resolution and resentment. The Stoics were right to see the animus as a faculty that needs governance. Without reason it becomes mere force; with reason it becomes virtue.

In a world that often celebrates intensity without direction, Animus asks what we are directing our spirit toward. Mindless courage is recklessness; mindful courage is the foundation of justice.
lore.originalScriptNote: Animus is a Latin word. It has no 'original script' in the sense of Greek or cuneiform; its canonical form is the Latin spelling animus. The ASCII form animus already represents the Latin spelling exactly. The restoration Animus is therefore the capitalised proper-noun citation form, not a phonetic recovery. The appropriate label is 'Scholarly Transliteration' or simply 'Latin'.

lore.archaeology: No altar to Animus is known — the word never had a cult — but the concept has a material footprint. Polybius, explaining Roman power to Greeks, describes the aristocratic funeral: the corpse arrayed in the forum with actors wearing the wax portrait-masks (imagines) of every ancestor, each mask a stored animus brought back to embody the dead (Histories 6.53–54). The Roman portrait tradition — the veristic busts of the Republic and thousands of funerary inscriptions commending the animus to the gods — is the largest surviving archive of the idea. Roman coins personified virtus and fides; what they struck in bronze was the disciplined animus itself, made payable.
